title: Iris's Unexpected Grand Opening
markdown:
Percy the steam engine chose his own first note. Not the Welcome Whistles Iris had timed to the second, but a mighty TOOT that shoved a colossal plume of steam straight into the Ribbon of Welcome. The ribbon sagged like a daisy left in a pocket. The glass roof of the Grand Tram Depot still held morning like a jewel. Visitors had only begun to trickle. Then the hush, then the gasp, then a little boy in the front row bouncing as if the day had been invented for him.

“Brilliant. A real surprise blast.”

Iris the deer, botanical illustrator and author of a Joyful Blueprint so complete it included the angle of sunbeams, felt her antlers droop a fraction. The scroll in her hoof listed a series of elegant greetings. It did not list this.

Yara the mole, older sister and finder of sideways solutions, nudged her hoof. “Do not fret. They think you meant it. Pizzazz.”

The plan is still excellent, Iris told herself. Reality is only being overfamiliar.

She managed a smile that had not yet decided to be true, and let the show go on because shows, unlike ribbons, refuse to be rescheduled. Next: the seating chart, weeks of names and tiny floral motifs. She stepped back to admire it. A terrier, escaped and delighted, zipped across the polish, snagged a corner with its tail, and dragged the masterpiece a few feet, leaving crumpled daisies in a trail that would have looked, in one of Iris’s wilder sketches, like a migration.

“Good doggy,” a woman chortled. “A playful flourish. The layout feels alive.”

Iris’s jaw gave a tiny tremor. That had been a botanical centrepiece on the interconnectedness of the community. Yara’s nose twitched. “They are loving it. The plan is still excellent. Reality is only being overfamiliar.”

Iris could have called a halt, fetched tape, restored every name to its ordained chair. She looked at the laughing woman and the unrepentant terrier and chose, instead, to leave the flourish where it had fallen and move to the vintage tram.

A volunteer, eager as a loose wheel, tripped over a toolbox. Foil-wrapped chocolates rained into the crowd. Cheers, not dismay. People went to their knees as if the floor had become a festival. Iris’s demonstration of the tram’s workings—rehearsed until the brass knew her voice—was then interrupted by a sing-along that started because the wood and metal looked, to the visitors, like an invitation. Her lines blurred. Her schedule shredded itself merrily. Artistic intention kept being read as accident, and accident as gift.

A late sun-stripe cut the depot floor and lit a chalk-dust path from an earlier planning line. It shimmered like something she might once have drawn on purpose.

She might have vanished into a timetable and called the day a failure. She might have scolded the volunteer and silenced the song. She stood in the gold dust instead and felt the old need for control loosen, not vanish, only loosen, the way a too-tight ribbon loosens when steam has been honest with it.

Yara, with a rumbling chuckle, unearthed a forgotten wooden box from a dusty corner. “The first tram driver’s,” she announced, voice carrying farther than a mole’s voice had any right to. “He rang these brass bells for all aboard, miles away.” She rang them. The melody was joyous and slightly off-key and entirely itself. Visitors clapped and hummed. Chocolate wrappers winked. The sagging ribbon, seen from here, looked like a wave.

Iris looked at the whole beautiful mess: droop, scatter, song, dust, bells. It was more alive than the sterile plan could have been. The setbacks had not ruined a display. They had asked people in.

“Yara,” she said, and the smile that arrived reached her eyes. “The plan was not only mine, was it?”

Yara winked. “Never is. A blueprint is the start. The splash of colour is everyone else.”

The plan is still excellent. Reality is only being overfamiliar.

Iris let the refrain stand without correcting it. She did not restore the ribbon to tautness. She did not recapture the terrier’s daisies. She let Percy keep his toot as the opening note of a day that had learned to sing. The Grand Tram Depot was open, and grandness, it turned out, had been a shared instrument all along.
characters: Iris (deer botanical illustrator), Yara (mole older sister)
author: StoryGen Community
